Seven participants were unmedicated; all participants met criteria for disruptive mood dysregulation disorder.

description.value: On valid money or no-money trials in the frustration condition, a correct response was followed by positive feedback on 40% of correct trials: “You win” for money trials or “Good job” for no-money trials. Money trials awarded 50¢; no-money trials involved no monetary gain or loss.

description.value: On valid money or no-money trials in the frustration condition, 60% of correct responses, irrespective of actual reaction time, were followed by misleading negative feedback (“Too slow”), inducing frustration. Money trials involved possible winning or losing of 50¢; no-money trials involved no monetary gain or loss.

spans.text: Frustration was induced by giving participants the feedback that they were “too slow” on 60% of accurate trials, irrespective of the subject’s reaction time

using a response button box

instructions.value: Identify the target’s location as quickly and accurately as possible using a response button box. During the frustration game, participants were told they must respond both quickly and accurately to win money and that adequate speed was based on a complicated formula considering performance on prior trials.

spans.text: Participants identified the target’s location as quickly and accurately as possible using a response button box.

stimuli.value: Fixation cross, trial-type symbol indicating money or no-money, two white squares, a blue spatial cue appearing in one square, a black target appearing in one square, and feedback. Money trials used green dollar signs and coin images; no-money trials used yellow circles.
